analysis.one_liner: Subjects guns and ammunition to federal consumer-safety rules, recalls, and lawsuits for the first time.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House subcommittee without a hearing or vote, after being referred there in June 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: Firearms are one of the few consumer products with no federal safety regulator. This bill would have given the Attorney General power to set design and manufacturing safety rules for guns and ammunition, order recalls or refunds of defective or unreasonably risky products, inspect factories and dealer records, fine violators, and let private citizens sue. It also required the government to collect and publish data on gun injuries and deaths. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people exposed to firearm injuries and deaths: the bill aimed to protect them the way other consumer products are protected — through safety standards, recalls of defective designs, public injury data, and lawsuits against makers of dangerous products. Buyers could have compared the safety of different guns and been warned or refunded when a product was defective [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun owners, buyers, and people exposed to gun injuries

how_it_helps.text: The bill required the Attorney General to write safety regulations for the design, manufacture, and performance of firearm products to reduce unreasonable risk of injury, modeled on how other consumer products are regulated [S2] [S3].

It let the government order recalls, repairs, replacements, refunds, and public warnings for defective or unreasonably risky firearm products, and to bar manufacture or sale of products that stay dangerously unsafe [S2] [S3].
It created a private right to sue violators for damages and to enforce the law in court, with attorney's fees available to prevailing plaintiffs [S3].

It required federal collection of firearm injury and death data, safety research, and annual public reporting, reversing the practical effect of earlier limits on federal firearm-safety research [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers and dealers, who would bear the cost of testing, certification, labeling, record-keeping, inspections, recalls, civil fines of up to $20,000 per violation, possible criminal penalties of up to two years, and private lawsuits [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Firearm and ammunition makers and dealers

drawbacks.text: Opponents argued the bill gave the Attorney General sweeping discretion to declare any firearm 'unreasonably risky' and ban its manufacture or sale, which they said could function as a backdoor ban on guns regardless of a product's safety record [S3].

Manufacturers would face per-product fines, recall costs, and new litigation exposure; honest supporters would acknowledge that some of those costs, especially small dealers' compliance costs, could be passed on to buyers [S3].

The bill applied to ammunition and even nonpowder guns like BB guns, raising the practical question of whether a law-enforcement agency rather than a safety agency could handle design regulation for tens of millions of firearms already in circulation [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have extended to guns the same basic consumer protections — safety standards, recalls, injury data, and legal accountability — that every other household product already has, at the cost of real compliance and litigation burdens on the firearm industry and some risk of overbroad discretionary bans. The core tradeoff was public safety gains against industry costs, not new restrictions on lawful ownership or use.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its crime subcommittee for the rest of the Congress and never got a hearing, a mark-up, or a vote in either chamber.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 10, 2003 by Rep. Patrick Kennedy with eight original cosponsors and referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1] [S3] [S5].
Two weeks later, on June 25, 2003, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security [S5].
No further action was ever taken; the bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, who kept their unique exemption from federal consumer product safety regulation, with no testing, recall, or lawsuit requirements taking effect.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or floor consideration; it died in committee.

against.name: House Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction after June 25, 2003 referral
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for the rest of the Congress without a hearing or vote, per the complete action history.

against.name: Firearm industry and gun-rights groups
against.role: Opponents of federal firearm design regulation
against.what_they_did: Opposed subjecting firearms to consumer product safety regulation, arguing it would enable bans on guns through the safety-approval process.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 12 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill was buried in a committee controlled by Republicans; no Republican supported it on the record.

industries.note: Firearms are the only major consumer product exempt from federal safety regulation; the bill would have ended that, subjecting makers to testing, certification, labeling, recall orders, inspections, fines, and lawsuits. The industry's interest in staying exempt runs against the public's interest in safer products.

industries.industry: Firearm and ammunition dealers and pawnbrokers
industries.note: Dealers would face record-keeping and inspection requirements, recall obligations, and liability for selling nonconforming products [S3].
Buyers would get labeled, tested products, safety information, recalls and refunds for defects, and a private right to sue — the same protections consumers of other products already have [S2] [S3].
